chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim from Muhammad ibn Isa from Yunus, from one who narrated it, said:

«Rights are extracted through four modes: the testimony of two just men. «If they are not two men, then one man and two women.» If there are not two women, then one man and the oath of the claimant. If there is no witness, then the oath is upon the defendant. If he does not swear, the oath is returned to the claimant, and it is obligatory upon him to swear and take his right. If he refuses to swear, then he has nothing.».
ai.seo_question: What is the hierarchy of evidence for establishing legal rights in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* details the jurisprudential hierarchy for establishing legal rights, moving from the strongest evidence (two just witnesses) to the weakest (defendant's oath), reflecting the Shia emphasis on procedural justice and evidentiary weight. It underscores the principle of *al-yamin* (oath) as a decisive tool when testimony is insufficient, ensuring that claims are resolved through a structured escalation of proof. The ruling highlights the defendant's obligation to swear if they deny a valid claim, with the consequence of losing the case if they refuse, thereby protecting the claimant's right.
